newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Shell, Elf set $4.0 bln N.Sea gas projects.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Shell, Elf set $4.0 bln N.Sea gas projects.

text.p: Britain formally approved a plan on Tuesday for a new gas pipeline from the North Sea to the English east coast, clearing the way for Royal Dutch/Shell and Elf to place initial contracts to develop three fields.
The firms said their total investment costs for all three fields would be about 2.5 billion pounds ($4.0 billion), once full approval was given, probably in early 1997.

With clearance for their plans to build a pipeline to Bacton, Norfolk, on the English east coast for land gas and condensate from the Shearwater, Elgin and Franklin fields, the firms placed key construction contracts for platforms.

Shell said it was awarding a contract worth over 300 million pounds to a consortium led by consruction and engineering group AMEC Plc to design, procure, build install and hook up the main Shearwater processing platform.
AMEC's Wallsend yard will build the main topsides, bridge and flare boom for Shearwater and Dutch privately-owned Heerema at Hartlepool will share the fabrication work on the contract.
Two Scottish yard groups are chasing a 400 million pound main process platform contract for the Elgin/Franklin project, the Department of Trade and Industry said in a statement.

"Only Scottish yards are left in contention for the main process platform (for Elgin/Franklin). The Barmac yard at Nigg is in competition with a consortium comprising Kvaerner John Brown at Methil and UIE Clydebank for this contract," it said.
Operator Elf is also due to award a further 90 million pound wellhead topsides contract for the twin fields.
While the companies and the government emphasised that development of the fields would secure jobs in England and Scotland, the news also affected the wider gas market.

The plan to route the three fields' product pipeline into Bacton, rather than the more northerly Teeside industrial area, is linked to wider plans for an international gas pipeline, known as the Interconnector, linking Norfolk and Belgium.
French-owned Elf is a shareholder in the Interconnector.
Shell said the Bacton link was the key to the development going ahead. "Without this new transport route to Bacton, development of Shearwater would not have proceeded," it said.
Shearwater, planned to come on stream in 2000, should have production rates reaching some 400 million cubic feet of gas per day and 90,000 barrles of condensate per day.
British Gas Plc's gas transport and storage arm TransCo had called for Britain to recommend a landing for the gas at Teeside,claiming there would be greater economic benefits.
It also said there was a strong argument for Shell and Elf to link their gas output into the existing Central Area Transmission System (CATS).

In an apparent compromise gesture, Shell said that it could envisage providing a stream of "chemicals feedstock, routed through a new pipeline link to the CATS to Teeside, depending on further demand in that location."
